source_title: In the shadows | Anmol Sidhu's 'Flowers of Acacia' - India Today
source_excerpt: A makeshift Punjab wedding stage. A young woman sways before 50 men, many of them high, several leering. To them, she is indispensable decor. To a boy in Kauloke village, she was something else. “As a child, when I saw these girls on stage, they seemed almost like ghosts to me, as the women in my house weren’t that ‘brave’ to dance in front of so many men,” remembers filmmaker Anmol Sidhu. That idea became Flowers of Acacia (Kikkran De Phull), Sidhu’s second feature after Jaggi (2022), on Punjab’s wedding orchestra dancers. Premiered at the New York Indian Film Festival’s Centrepiece Special Night and nominated for Best Indie Film in Melbourne, its India premiere is at the Dharamshala International Film Festival.A dancer’s death by bullet at a wedding stunned Sidhu, and he began travelling with orchestra groups in 2022. “Every girl I met wanted her story to be told,” he says. They came from Bengal, Himachal and beyond, hence the Punjabi, Bengali and Hindi dialects in the movie. Shooting at real weddings was tough, says Sidhu; actors first danced there to acclimatise, and Bhangra novices trained for six months. The camera stays wide, avoiding close-ups; viewers sense a documentary’s shadow, which he accepts. There is no redemptive ending: “Life doesn’t always have a happy ending. No matter how hard I try, I can't make my stories unrealistic.”Punjabi cinema, Sidhu notes, is comedies, songs and NRI fantasy, yet Jaggi reached many in Punjab, proving an audience exists. “We need to make more films that aren't slapstick comedies,” he adds. Another Punjab-set film awaits, with post-production nearly done.- Ends
